subsystems.name: Flexible substrate and encapsulation
subsystems.role: Provides a compliant, skin-like base and protects the delicate sensors from moisture, dirt and mechanical wear.

subsystems.name: Tactile sensor array
subsystems.role: Detects pressure, shear and vibration, mimicking the mechanoreceptors in human skin.

subsystems.name: Temperature and other sensors
subsystems.role: Adds thermal and sometimes humidity sensing to give a fuller picture of contact.

subsystems.name: Readout and signal processing
subsystems.role: Converts tiny analog sensor signals into digital data that a robot or prosthetic can use.

subsystems.name: Stretchable interconnects
subsystems.role: Routes power and signals across the skin without breaking when it bends or stretches.

subsystems.name: Power and data interface
subsystems.role: Supplies power and transmits sensor data to the host system.

buildSteps.title: Design the sensor layout
buildSteps.detail: Choose the sensing principle (capacitive, piezoelectric, etc.), the density of sensor pixels, and the flexible materials that will carry them.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the flexible substrate
buildSteps.detail: Spin-coat or laminate a thin polymer film such as polyimide or PDMS onto a rigid carrier wafer for handling.

buildSteps.title: Pattern electrodes and interconnects
buildSteps.detail: Use photolithography, inkjet printing or laser ablation to create fine metal traces and electrode arrays on the substrate.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the sensing layers
buildSteps.detail: Deposit or transfer the active sensor materials — for example, a microstructured elastomer for capacitive sensing or piezoelectric nanowires.

buildSteps.title: Build the readout electronics
buildSteps.detail: Either pattern organic transistors directly on the skin or bond ultra-thin silicon chips to amplify and multiplex the signals.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate and passivate
buildSteps.detail: Apply protective polymer layers that seal out moisture and ions while remaining flexible enough to bend with the skin.

buildSteps.title: Test and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Measure sensitivity, dynamic range, response time and durability under repeated bending and stretching.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with the host
buildSteps.detail: Connect the skin to a power source and data link, then attach it to a robot gripper, prosthetic limb or wearable device.

prerequisites.why: Polyimide and PDMS substrates and serpentine metal traces are already used in flexible displays and sensors.
They can be printed on plastic but are slower and less stable than silicon, limiting high-speed readout.
Capacitive and piezoelectric arrays have been demonstrated in labs, but scaling to large areas with high resolution is difficult.
Liquid metal and conductive polymer interconnects work in prototypes but degrade after many cycles.
Thin-film batteries and wireless power are available, but energy density and safety need improvement for body-worn use.
To give a prosthetic user feeling, the skin's signals must connect to nerves — a field still in early clinical trials.

pathway.milestone: Small-area lab prototypes with a few hundred sensor pixels
pathway.unlocks: Basic tactile sensing for robotic grippers and simple touch screens.

pathway.milestone: Large-area, high-resolution skins with integrated flexible readout
pathway.unlocks: Robots that can handle delicate objects and detect slip.

pathway.milestone: Durable, stretchable skins with wireless power and data
pathway.unlocks: Prosthetic limbs that provide realistic touch feedback to the user.
Artificial skin for burn victims and full-body sensing for humanoid robots.
